title: How to Optimize for AI Search: How Google and AI Choose Which Answers to Show
summary: Learn how Google, AI search, and voice assistants choose which answers to show—and how small businesses can improve visibility in AI-driven search results.
body_markdown:
Key Takeaways


##


1. AI search is changing how customers discover and evaluate local businesses.
2. To optimize for AI search, make your website content clear, specific, useful, and easy for search systems to interpret.
3. Keep your business information accurate and consistent across your website, Google Business Profile, directories, social profiles, and other relevant sources.
4. Reviews, local content, images, video, and other real-world signals can give AI systems more context about your business.
5. Traditional SEO still matters because AI search experiences rely on many of the same technical and content foundations.
6. Measure visibility beyond traditional rankings by watching impressions, engagement, conversions, and emerging generative AI performance data where available.


## What Does It Mean to Optimize for AI Search?


[Optimizing for AI search](https://www.thryv.com/blog/ai-content-optimization-for-small-business/) means creating and maintaining an online presence that helps AI-powered search systems accurately understand your business and determine when it is relevant to a customer’s question.


That includes more than adding keywords to a website.


AI search can look across your website and other publicly available information to understand things such as:


- What your business does
- Which products or services you offer
- Where you operate
- Who you serve
- What makes your business different
- Whether your business appears trustworthy and established
- What customers say about their experiences
- Whether your business information is consistent across sources


Google’s current guidance makes an important point: there isn’t a separate set of magic tricks for ranking in[AEO search](https://www.thryv.com/blog/answer-engine-optimization-shorten-customer-decision-journey/) . The same fundamentals that help content perform in traditional Search continue to matter in AI experiences.


That means the goal isn’t to write content specifically for a machine. It’s to make your business information so clear and useful that both people and search systems can understand it.

## How AI Search Chooses Which Answers to Show


AI-powered search experiences can[use information from multiple sources](https://www.thryv.com/blog/local-aeo-best-practices-small-businesses-2026-webinar-recap/) to build a response to a customer’s question.


For example, someone might search:


“What’s the best HVAC company near me for emergency repairs?”


The system needs to understand several things at once. It needs to identify businesses that offer HVAC services, determine which ones serve the searcher’s area, understand whether emergency repairs are available, and evaluate information that helps establish relevance and trust.


That makes **context** increasingly important.


A business that simply says “We’re the best HVAC company” gives search systems very little useful information.


A business that clearly explains:


- Emergency HVAC repair
- Service areas
- Types of systems serviced
- Hours of operation
- Common problems handled
- Customer experiences
- Credentials or experience
- How to contact the business


provides much stronger context.


### 1. Start With Clear, Specific Website Content


The first step to optimize for AI search is making your website easy to understand.


Avoid relying on vague marketing language such as “quality solutions for all your needs.” Instead, clearly explain what you offer and who you serve.


Your website should make it easy to answer questions such as:


**What do you do?**


Clearly describe your primary products or services.


**Who do you serve?**


Identify your ideal customers or the industries you work with.


**Where do you operate?**


List relevant cities, neighborhoods, regions, or service areas.


**What problems do you solve?**


Explain the situations that lead customers to look for your business.


**Why should customers choose you?**


Highlight meaningful differentiators, experience, credentials, processes, or customer benefits.


This type of specificity helps both customers and search systems understand your business.


Google’s guidance specifically recommends creating unique, valuable content rather than generic information that could apply to any business.


### 2. Create Content Around Real Customer Questions


Customers don’t always search using the exact language found on a service page.


They ask questions.


For example:


- How much does a roof replacement cost?
- Do I need an emergency plumber?
- How long does a dental cleaning take?
- What should I look for in a personal injury attorney?
- Does this salon offer same-day appointments?


To optimize for AI search, build useful content around the questions your customers actually ask.


Use headings that clearly describe the topic, then provide direct answers before expanding with additional context.


This structure can make your content easier for people to scan and easier for search systems to interpret.


But don’t create dozens of nearly identical pages simply to target slightly different questions. Google’s current guidance continues to emphasize original, helpful content and warns against creating large amounts of low-value content primarily for search visibility.


### 3. Strengthen Your Business Entity and Local Signals


AI search needs to understand not only your content, but also **which business that content belongs to** .


That’s why your business information should be consistent across the web.


Check your:


- Business name
- Address or service area
- Phone number
- Website
- Hours
- Services
- Business categories
- Google Business Profile
- Online directories
- Social profiles
- Industry-specific profiles


If your website says you are open until 8 p.m., but another important listing says 5 p.m., you’ve created uncertainty.


Consistent information and[accurate business listings](https://www.thryv.com/blog/better-business-listings/) gives search systems more reliable context about your business.


For local businesses, this is especially important because AI-powered recommendations can depend on understanding both the business and its local search relevance.

### 4. Treat Reviews as Firsthand Context


Reviews aren’t just a reputation management tool. They can provide firsthand context about the customer experience.


A service page might tell someone that a business offers “fast plumbing repairs.”


Customer[online reviews](https://www.thryv.com/blog/why-online-reviews-matter-local-seo/) can provide additional context about what “fast” actually means.


Customers might mention:


- Emergency response times
- Specific services performed
- Neighborhoods served
- Products or brands used
- Communication quality
- Pricing experiences
- The types of problems the business solved


That real-world language can help reinforce what a business does and how customers experience it.


The goal isn’t to stuff keywords into reviews. Instead, make it easy for satisfied customers to honestly describe their experience.


And remember:[authentic reviews matter](https://www.thryv.com/blog/why-reviews-matter-for-ai-search/) . Google’s guidance continues to emphasize quality and trustworthy information, while its 2026 documentation has also tightened guidance around fake and undisclosed incentivized reviews.


### 5. Add Images and Video to Your Content


AI search isn’t limited to text.


Google’s current AI search guidance highlights the importance of supporting text with high-quality images and video as[search becomes increasingly multimodal](https://www.thryv.com/blog/answer-engine-optimization-business-visibility-ai-search/) .


For a local business, that could mean adding:


- Photos of your team
- Before-and-after project images
- Product demonstrations
- Service videos
- Walkthroughs
- How-to videos
- Photos of your location
- Images showing completed work


Don’t treat visual content as decoration. Give images useful filenames and descriptive alt text, and make sure the surrounding page content explains what users are seeing.


For example, instead of a generic image caption such as “Our work,” explain what the image demonstrates.


### 6. Use Structured Data to Reinforce What Your Page Says


Structured data gives search engines machine-readable information about your page.


It can help communicate details such as the type of organization, business information, products, services, events, or other supported content.


The important part is accuracy.


Your structured data should reflect information that is actually visible on the page. Google specifically recommends ensuring that structured data matches the visible content and follows its guidelines.


Structured data isn’t a shortcut to AI visibility. Think of it as another way to make your existing information easier for search systems to interpret.


### 7. Don’t Forget Traditional SEO


One of the biggest misconceptions about AI search is that businesses need to choose between[SEO and AI optimization](https://www.thryv.com/blog/seo-for-small-businesses/) .


You don’t.


Google’s latest guidance explicitly reinforces that SEO best practices remain foundational to visibility in generative AI search experiences.


That means you should still:


- Use descriptive page titles and headings
- Create useful internal links
- Make pages crawlable and indexable
- Optimize page speed and mobile usability
- Use descriptive URLs
- Write useful meta descriptions
- Keep important content accessible to search engines
- Fix broken links and technical issues
- Build authoritative, relevant content


Before an AI system can understand and potentially use your content, it needs to be able to access and process it.

### 8. Build a Consistent Presence Beyond Your Website


Your website is important, but it[isn’t the only source of information](https://www.thryv.com/blog/off-page-seo-small-businesses/) about your business.


AI systems can encounter information across different parts of the web. That makes your broader digital presence increasingly important.


Look for opportunities to maintain accurate information on relevant:


- Business directories
- Industry websites
- Review platforms
- Social media profiles
- Local organizations
- Community websites
- Professional associations
- News or media coverage


The goal isn’t to be everywhere.


It’s to make sure the places where customers and search systems are likely to encounter your business tell a consistent story.


### 9. Create Content That Adds Something New


AI can summarize information that already exists. That makes original insight even more valuable.


Instead of rewriting the same generic advice found across dozens of websites, add something that demonstrates real experience.


For example:


- Share lessons from completed projects.
- Explain common customer mistakes.
- Answer questions your team hears repeatedly.
- Show real before-and-after examples.
- Provide original data or observations.
- Explain how your process works.
- Share expert perspectives from people on your team.


Google’s current guidance emphasizes content that is unique, useful, and non-commodity rather than content that simply repeats information already available elsewhere.


### 10. Measure More Than Rankings


AI search changes how visibility should be measured.


A traditional SEO report might focus heavily on keyword rankings and organic traffic. Those metrics still matter, but they don’t tell the entire story.


Look at:


- Organic impressions
- Click-through rate
- Website engagement
- Leads
- Calls
- Form submissions
- Appointment requests
- Conversion rates
- Branded searches
- Local visibility
- Search queries driving traffic


Google also began rolling out dedicated Search Console reporting for visibility within generative AI features in 2026, including AI Overviews and AI Mode. The reporting is initially available to a subset of sites as Google continues testing and expanding it.


As these reporting capabilities evolve, businesses will have more ways to understand how their content performs across traditional and AI-powered search.


## What About Voice Search?


Voice search still matters, but it is no longer useful to think about voice as an entirely separate optimization strategy.


People increasingly use[conversational language when searching](https://www.thryv.com/blog/near-me-search-local-seo-opportunities/) , whether they’re speaking to a voice assistant or typing a detailed question into an AI-powered search experience.


That makes conversational, question-based content useful across multiple search formats.


Instead of trying to optimize separately for every device, focus on answering real customer questions clearly.


A page that answers “How often should I have my HVAC system serviced?” can potentially serve a customer whether they type the question, speak it aloud, or ask an AI-powered search experience.


## What Small Businesses Should Do Now


If you want to optimize for AI search, don’t start by rebuilding your entire website.


Start with the fundamentals.


**First, audit your business information.** Make sure your name, services, location, hours, phone number, and other core details are accurate everywhere customers may find you.


**Next, review your website.** Can someone quickly understand what you do, where you operate, who you serve, and why customers choose you?


**Then, identify customer questions.** Turn the questions your team hears every day into useful website content.


**Strengthen your reputation.** Encourage genuine customer reviews and respond thoughtfully to feedback.


**Add real-world context.** Use original photos, videos, examples, and insights that demonstrate your experience.


**Finally, keep measuring.** Watch both traditional SEO metrics and emerging AI search visibility data as reporting becomes more available.

## The Future of Search Is About Being the Best Answer


AI search is changing how customers discover businesses, but the fundamentals haven’t disappeared.


Businesses still need to be relevant. They still need to be trustworthy. Their websites still need to work. Their information still needs to be accurate.


What’s changing is how that information gets interpreted and delivered.


Instead of simply competing to rank for a keyword, businesses increasingly need to make their entire digital presence clear enough for search systems to understand.


When your website, listings, reviews, social profiles, and other online signals consistently communicate what your business does and why customers trust you, you give AI-powered search more reliable information to work with.


**That’s what it means to optimize for AI search: make your business easy to understand, easy to verify, and genuinely useful to the customers you’re trying to reach.**
